passage: At the Saturday swimming club, Harish, eleven, started changing in the toilet cubicle instead of the changing room. He kept his towel round his shoulders at the pool edge and snapped at his friend who asked why. When his voice cracked mid-shout during a relay, two boys laughed, and Harish went red and sat out. Coach Ganga found him by the lockers. "Voice cracking, new hair, body feeling strange?" she asked quietly. Harish stared at the floor, then nodded. "That's puberty. Every body does it, just at different times. Your voice is growing up. Nothing is wrong with you." She said the cubicle was fine to use for as long as he liked. Next week he was back in the relay, still a bit pink.

qa.q: Where did Harish start changing?
qa.a: In the toilet cubicle.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when the boys laughed at his voice?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and self-conscious, going red and sitting out.

qa.q: What did Coach Ganga's words achieve, and why?
qa.a: Her plain, calm explanation that puberty happens to everyone at different times eased his shame, and he returned to the relay.

qa.q: How might Harish's friend have felt when Harish snapped?
qa.a: Confused and a bit hurt, not knowing Harish was embarrassed about his changing body.

grounding: Shows a child starting puberty turning embarrassed, moody and self-conscious, and a simple honest explanation reducing the shame.

passage: I'm Irfan, and my cousin Nikita has lived with us since she was little. This year something changed. She's ten, and suddenly she wears my old baggy hoodies even in the heat, hunches her shoulders and won't go to swimming class. On Sunday she burst into tears because my Ammi said, "Look how tall you're getting!" Then she shouted at me for nothing and slammed her door. I don't know what's going on inside her head; I'm her cousin, not a mind-reader. But that night Ammi sat with her and a simple book about growing up, and I heard them talking softly for a long time. Nikita came out for dinner still in a hoodie, but laughing at my bad jokes again.

qa.q: What does Nikita wear even in the heat?
qa.a: Irfan's old baggy hoodies.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she cried at the comment about getting tall?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and self-conscious about her changing body, so even a friendly remark felt like too much.

qa.q: What helped Nikita, and why?
qa.a: Ammi sitting with her and a simple book about growing up; calm, honest explanations reduce shame.

qa.q: How does Irfan make sense of the change in Nikita?
qa.a: Irfan notices the hoodies, the tears and the slammed door, but admits to not knowing what is going on inside her head.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose body is starting to change becoming self-conscious and moody, and honest, simple explanations easing the shame.

passage: When Ujjwal read aloud in Class 6, his voice cracked in the middle of "photosynthesis", squeaky then deep. Dhruv snorted, and half the class laughed. At home in their Indore flat, Ujjwal slammed his bag down, refused dinner, and shut himself in the bathroom, where he noticed again the new smell under his arms and the dark fuzz on his lip. His body felt like someone else's. Papa knocked. "Ujju, can I come in? I remember this." He sat on the edge of the tub and explained simply: voices crack while they deepen, sweat changes, hair grows, and it happens to everyone in their own time. "Nothing's wrong with you. It's puberty. We'll get you a deodorant tomorrow." Ujjwal came out and ate two rotis.

qa.q: Which word made Ujjwal's voice crack?
qa.a: Photosynthesis.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he shut himself in the bathroom?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, as if his changing body belonged to someone else.

qa.q: Why did Papa's explanation help?
qa.a: It was honest and simple, told Ujjwal nothing was wrong, and offered a practical step, which eased his shame.

qa.q: How might Papa feel remembering his own changes?
qa.a: He likely feels tender and understanding, remembering how awkward it was for him.

grounding: Shows a child in early puberty feeling embarrassed and moody as his body changes, and an honest, simple explanation reducing the shame.

passage:
"Dhruv, why are you wearing a full-sleeve jacket in May?"
"Leave me alone, Sunaina Didi."
"You've worn it for a week. Are you cold?"
"No. There's hair. On my arms. And under. It's gross."
"Oh, Dhru. It's not gross. It's growing up."
"Nobody else in my class has it."
"Somebody always starts first. By next year lots of them will. I got pimples before anyone in my class, remember?"
"You cried about it."
"I did. Then Mumma told me what was happening and bought me face wash, and it felt less weird. Want me to tell you what else is coming?"
"Like what?"
"Voice changes, more sweat, feeling cross for no reason. All normal. Ask me anything. I won't laugh."
"Promise?"
"Promise. Now take that jacket off before you melt."

qa.q: What month is it?
qa.a: May.

qa.q: Why is Dhruv wearing a jacket?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and self-conscious about the new hair on his arms and wants to hide it.

qa.q: What makes Sunaina's talk helpful?
qa.a: She explains simply, shares her own experience, promises not to laugh, and offers to tell him what's coming, which reduces the shame.

qa.q: How does Sunaina remember her own early changes?
qa.a: She remembers crying about pimples and feeling less weird once Mumma explained, so she understands how Dhruv feels.

grounding: Shows a child embarrassed and self-conscious about early body changes, and an honest, simple explanation from an older sister easing the shame.

passage: Last year, when I was ten, my body started changing before my friends' did. My chest felt sore and looked different, and I began hunching over in PE so nobody would notice. I snapped at everyone and cried over small things. I thought something was wrong with me. Then Farida Aunty, my mother's friend who is a nurse, came to stay. She noticed the hunching and asked me gently. She showed me pictures in a book and explained that it was puberty, that it starts at different times for everyone, and that it's normal. She took me to buy soft vests. I still felt shy. But I stopped hunching, and I stopped thinking I was broken. I'm Aparna, and now I tell my younger cousin the truth when she asks.

qa.q: What did Farida Aunty take Aparna to buy?
qa.a: Soft vests.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel before Farida Aunty explained?
qa.a: Aparna felt embarrassed, moody and scared that something was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Farida Aunty's explanation help?
qa.a: It was honest and calm and used a book, showing the changes were normal puberty that starts at different times, which eased the shame.

qa.q: How might Aparna's friends have seen the hunching and snapping?
qa.a: They may have thought Aparna was just grumpy, not knowing about the worry underneath.

grounding: Shows a child whose body starts changing early feeling embarrassed and self-conscious, and a simple, honest explanation reducing shame.

passage:
School nurse's note, Class 5, Monday
Avni came to the sick room at lunch saying she had a stomach ache, but mostly she wanted to hide. Her class teacher says she has started wearing her sweater all day in the heat and snaps at friends who tease her for growing taller than the boys. When I asked gently, she whispered that her chest is changing, she hates it, and her body feels like it belongs to someone else. I told her plainly that bodies start changing at different times, that it is normal and nothing to be ashamed of, and showed her a simple picture book about growing up. With her permission, I phoned her mother this afternoon so they can talk at home and shop for a comfortable vest together.
Jaya

qa.q: What did Avni say she had when she came to the sick room?
qa.a: A stomach ache.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about her changing body?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and self-conscious, as if her body belongs to someone else.

qa.q: What did Jaya do that reduced Avni's shame?
qa.a: Jaya explained plainly that bodies change at different times and that it's normal, showed a simple picture book, and with permission called her mother.

qa.q: How might the friends who tease see Avni's sweater?
qa.a: They may think it's strange or funny, not knowing Avni is trying to hide changes that feel embarrassing.

grounding: A child beginning puberty feels embarrassed and moody, and an honest, simple explanation from an adult reduces her shame.
